sections.title: Executive summary

summary.text: Summarises the WHO guideline on home-based records, defining them as household-kept paper or electronic health documents ranging from vaccination cards to integrated maternal and child health books, whose benefits had not been systematically reviewed. It outlines development under the WHO handbook process with GRADE and an evidence-to-decision framework, and presents two recommendations: using home-based records to complement facility records, and that evidence is insufficient to favour any particular type or design. It also lists remarks on low-certainty evidence, privacy of HIV information, sustainable financing and further research needs.

sections.extract: Executive summary Introduction A home-based record is a health document used to record the history of health services received by an individual. It is kept in the household, in either paper or electronic format, by the individual or their caregiver and is intended to be integrated into the health information system and complement records maintained by health facilities. sections.title: Home-based records: an overview

summary.text: Gives an overview of home-based records, describing their purpose in recording maternal, newborn and child health care and the different types in use, from maternal records and vaccination cards to integrated MCH books. It discusses their functions and global use and introduces the rationale and scope of the guideline. It ends by explaining how the priority questions and proximal and distal outcomes were chosen.

sections.extract: 1. Home-based records: an overview 1.1 Functions of home-based records A home-based record is a health document used to record the history of health services received by an individual. Its primary purpose is to record essential information related to maternal, newborn and child health (MNCH), including health status, visits to a health care provider, vaccinations received and the child’s growth and development. sections.title: Methods

summary.text: Describes how the guideline was developed according to the WHO handbook, including the roles of the WHO Steering Group, the 12-member Guideline Development Group, the Technical Working Group and external partners. It covers declarations of interest and the December 2016 scoping meeting that set six priority questions and outcomes. It explains evidence retrieval through systematic reviews, a qualitative evidence synthesis and a framework analysis of grey literature and key informant interviews, with certainty grading. It closes with the categories used for recommendations and the process of document preparation and peer review.

sections.extract: They comprised academics with expertise in guideline development, research or policy development related to home-based records, as well as international and country-level policy- makers and implementers of home-based record programmes. This diverse group was drawn from every WHO region, and efforts were made to ensure geographic representation and gender balance, and that they had no important conflicts of interest.

sections.title: Recommendations and evidence on home-based records for MNCH

summary.text: Presents the two recommendations on home-based records, with the rationale that although evidence certainty was low and studies were few, old and varied, benefits outweighed harms given positive effects on several care-seeking, home care and communication outcomes and use in at least 163 countries. It reviews the quantitative and qualitative evidence for each priority question, including values, acceptability, equity, resources and feasibility. Remarks address design, privacy and sustainable financing. The section ends with the evidence-to-decision framework table rating effects, certainty, costs, equity, acceptability and feasibility.

sections.title: Implementation considerations

summary.text: Sets out implementation considerations for home-based records, stressing planning and funding at every stage, government ownership, stakeholder involvement and harmonised content across health areas. It advises local adaptation and testing, design for low literacy, regular redesigns and attention to privacy. It also notes concerns about advertising on records and points to the Framework of Engagement with Non-State Actors for weighing risks.

sections.extract: Implementation considerations were derived from the framework analysis and were discussed within the GDG. Broadly, these deal with the content and design of home-based records, integration into health services and systems, costs, and addressing the needs of health workers, women and caregivers. sections.title: Research gaps

summary.text: Lists research gaps on home-based records, including the need for more and better-quality studies on health outcomes, standardised outcome measures and a logic model. It calls for research on effects on providers, comparisons of formats and electronic records, and cost-effectiveness of integrated records. It also identifies implementation questions such as design, durability, free versus paid distribution and incentive schemes.

sections.extract: During the guideline development process, the GDG identified gaps that need to be addressed in future research: 1. summary.text: Annex 5, detailing the evidence on effects of home-based records for each priority question, beginning with maternal care-seeking, care practices and morbidity in cluster trials of maternal and child health handbooks in Mongolia and Indonesia. It continues with newborn and child outcomes and with health service outcomes such as satisfaction and women's sense of control when holding their own notes, drawing on trials in the United Kingdom and Australia. Most effects are small or non-significant, with a few positive findings such as tetanus immunization, and certainty ranges from very low to moderate. tables.label: Table 1
tables.caption: Table 1. Recommendations on home-based records
rows: 1. The use of home-based records, as a complement to facility-based records, is recommended for the care of pregnant women, mothers, newborns and children, to improve care-seeking behaviours, male involvement and support in the household, maternal and child home care practices, infant and child feeding, and communication between health providers and women/caregivers. (Low-certainty evidence)

2. There was insufficient evidence available to determine if any specific type, format or design of home-based records is more effective. Policy-makers should involve stakeholders to discuss the important considerations with respect to type, content and implementation of home-based records.

The GDG considered the evidence presented and judged that, overall, the certainty of evidence of the effectiveness of home-based records was low. They recognized that the existing evidence base has limitations, including: the small number of studies found, half of which were conducted in high-income countries; the age of these, with some conducted before 2000; and the variety in the studies, which looked at different types of home-based records and measured a broad array of outcomes.

The impact varied by outcome. Some studies showed a positive effect on maternal health immunization care-seeking, outcomes related to a supportive home environment for maternal and child health (MCH) care, improved infant feeding and other child health care practices, improved child growth and development, improved continuity of care across MCH, and improved communication with health providers. However, there was also no significant effect reported on many maternal, newborn and child care-seeking and care practice outcomes. For many outcomes, no studies were found.

Although the evidence base has its limitations, the GDG determined that the desirable effects outweigh any undesirable effects, and also considered in their judgements the fact that home-based records have a long history and are implemented in at least 163 countries. Furthermore, they considered the qualitative evidence that reports women, caregivers and providers from a variety of settings value different forms of home-based records. The GDG also noted that home-based records contribute to a larger objective of ensuring the right to access to information, and are in line with global efforts for people-centred care, which WHO embraces.

In remote and fragile settings, where health systems are weak or where health information systems are absent or poor, and in locations where caregivers may use multiple health facilities, home-based records may be of greater value than in more developed settings and health systems.

Concerns about the privacy of online or electronic records were reported in studies. The GDG highlighted the potential sensitivity of information in home-based records on HIV testing, status or treatment. Careful consideration should be given as to what personal information is necessary to include in home-based records, to avoid stigma and discrimination.
Countries currently using home-based records should consider appropriate use, design and content, as well as sustainable financing to maximize their use and impact.

Additional research is needed on the benefits of using home-based records for recording information on single aspects of care, versus home-based records that include wider MNCH aspects for health education purposes. Evidence was not available at this time to inform this priority question for countries.

narratives.es: El cuadro resume las valoraciones del Grupo de Elaboración de Directrices sobre los criterios de la evidencia a la decisión para los registros domiciliarios: efectos deseables para cada pregunta prioritaria (P1–P6), efectos indeseables, certeza de la evidencia, valores, equilibrio de efectos, recursos, costoefectividad, equidad, aceptabilidad y viabilidad. Cada fila enumera las respuestas posibles, y la valoración del Grupo se marca con una X o en negrita.
narratives.fr: Le tableau résume les jugements du Groupe d’élaboration des lignes directrices sur les critères de passage des données probantes à la décision pour les dossiers tenus à domicile : effets souhaitables pour chaque question prioritaire (Q1–Q6), effets indésirables, degré de certitude des données, valeurs, équilibre des effets, ressources, coût-efficacité, équité, acceptabilité et faisabilité. Chaque ligne énumère les réponses possibles, le jugement du Groupe étant signalé par un X ou en gras.
narratives.ru: В таблице обобщены суждения Группы по разработке руководящих принципов по критериям перехода от фактических данных к решениям в отношении хранящихся на дому медицинских записей: желательные эффекты по каждому приоритетному вопросу (В1–В6), нежелательные эффекты, достоверность фактических данных, ценности, баланс эффектов, ресурсы, затратоэффективность, справедливость, приемлемость и осуществимость. В каждой строке перечислены возможные варианты ответа, а суждение Группы отмечено знаком X или выделено жирным шрифтом.
